item.title: When will MPO-listed teachers receive salary under new pay structure, what the ministry says
item.description:
Teachers and employees at private educational institutions covered by the Monthly Pay Order (MPO) scheme will also receive the benefits of the new national pay structure, alongside government employees.

However, while the process of implementing the new pay structure for government employees is already under way, it remains unclear when MPO-listed teachers and employees will receive their salaries under the revised structure.

The Ministry of Finance has issued a circular making the new pay structure effective for government employees from 1 July. They may receive three months’ arrears along with their October salaries. MPO-listed teachers and employees, however, may have to wait longer.

Officials concerned at the Ministry of Education said the Finance Division would issue the order on the matter.

An additional secretary of the Finance Division later told Prothom Alo that it was not yet possible to say when the order would be issued, as the matter involved a process that had to be completed.

The Ministry of Finance has issued a circular making the new pay structure effective for government employees from 1 July. They may receive three months’ arrears along with their October salaries. MPO-listed teachers and employees, however, may have to wait longer.

According to sources familiar with the matter, completing the process to pay MPO-listed teachers and employees under the new structure could take until November or December. However, the timeline will depend on when the Finance Division issues its order and how quickly the subsequent steps are completed.

Basic salaries and allowances to increase under new structure

More than 600,000 teachers and employees across the country are currently covered by the MPO scheme. Of them, around 400,000 are under the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, nearly 200,000 under the Directorate of Madrasah Education, and more than 23,000 under the Directorate of Technical Education.

The government provides monthly financial grants to cover the salaries and allowances of teachers and employees at private educational institutions under the MPO scheme. MPO stands for Monthly Pay Order. Those covered by the scheme receive 100 per cent of their basic salaries, along with certain allowances, including medical benefits.

Last year, the government decided to raise the house rent allowance for MPO-listed teachers and employees to 15 per cent of their basic salaries. Previously, they received Tk 1,000 a month as house rent allowance.

Some private educational institutions with substantial independent income provide additional payments to their staff beyond the MPO benefits. Most institutions, however, lack the financial capacity to do so. As a result, the timing of the new pay structure is particularly important for teachers and employees who depend on government grants.

Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel, DG, DSHEDiscussions were under way with the ministry to ensure that MPO-listed teachers and employees could receive their salaries and allowances under the new structure as soon as possible.

Once the new structure takes effect for them, MPO-listed teachers and employees will receive higher basic salaries and house rent allowances. Salary grades vary according to the level and type of institution, including schools and colleges. Under the revised structure, employees will be paid according to the grades they currently occupy.

For example, lecturers at private colleges will receive basic salaries under Grade 9, the same grade as lecturers at government colleges.

Under the new pay structure for government employees, basic salaries have been increased by between 100 per cent and 142 per cent, depending on the grade. The revised structure retains the existing 20 grades. The basic salary for Grade 20, the lowest grade, has been raised from Tk 8,250 to Tk 20,000, while the salary for Grade 1, the highest, has increased from Tk 78,000 to Tk 156,000.

The government plans to implement the new pay structure in phases from 1 July this year. Basic salaries are scheduled to be introduced in three phases between 1 July 2026 and 2027, while allowances are planned to take effect simultaneously from 1 January 2028.

However, no specific implementation deadline has been set for MPO-listed teachers and employees. They may therefore have to wait longer to receive their revised salaries and allowances.

Asked about the matter, Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel, director general of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, told Prothom Alo that discussions were under way with the ministry to ensure that MPO-listed teachers and employees could receive their salaries and allowances under the new structure as soon as possible.

item.title: Are we the offenders for defending ourselves, woman asks
item.description:
A 23-year-old woman who alleges that she was sexually harassed in Dhaka’s Dhanmondi area has said police at the scene did not help her, forcing her to call a relative for protection. When the relative confronted the man accused of harassing her and assaulted him, police detained the relative, who was later sentenced to 15 days in jail.

“Then are we the ones who have committed a crime by trying to protect myself?” the woman asked.

She made the remarks in a written message sent to Prothom Alo on Wednesday night. She said she had also posted the same statement on social media.

Police detained her relative, Khalid Hasan, 35, on Wednesday afternoon over his alleged involvement in the assault of a man on a footpath in Dhanmondi. He was later produced before the Special Metropolitan Magistrate Court of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Ramna zone, which sentenced him to 15 days in jail.

On Monday afternoon, Khalid had allegedly assaulted Shahid Abdullah Al Masud, also known as Masud Rana, 48, and forced him to perform sit-ups while holding his ears. The incident took place opposite Bangladesh Eye Hospital on Satmasjid Road in Dhanmondi, following allegations of sexual harassment. Later, Dhanmondi police detained Shahid Abdullah, who was sentenced to one month in jail by the DMP’s Special Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

A video of the assault went viral on social media, triggering widespread discussion and criticism. Questions were also raised about the role of two police officers present at the scene.

Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) Abdul Hai of Dhanmondi police station has already been withdrawn from his workplace over allegations of negligence of duty.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Wednesday, Dhanmondi police station Officer-in-Charge Muhammad Imdadul Islam Taiyeb said Abdul Hai had some responsibilities at the scene. He had been withdrawn from the station. The other two police personnel present belonged to the Public Order Management unit, he said, adding that he had no information about their cases.

In her statement, the woman said she was married. She referred to a recently circulated video showing a middle-aged man abusing and assaulting an older man. The older man, she said, had touched a relative of the man carrying out the assault inappropriately. She said she was the person who had been sexually harassed and that her relative had confronted the man over the unwanted touching.

The woman said she had remained silent until now because she did not want to appear in the media as a married woman or face disruption to her daily life. But she could no longer remain silent, she said, because people were blaming her relative and demanding punishment without knowing or understanding the full circumstances.

She said media coverage had added to her suffering and that she was now seeking help from the media.

“When a woman’s dignity is violated and the law does not help her, whom should she turn to?” she asked.

Young man detained over Dhaka footpath assault, inactive cop withdrawn

Referring to the two police officers visible in the video, the woman said she initially took the older man to law enforcement officers and demanded action against him. Police told her to file a case, she said, but at the time she was occupied with caring for a patient at a hospital.

She questioned whether it was reasonable to expect her to go and file a case in the middle of such a situation.

The woman said she and her relative repeatedly urged the older man to go to the police station, but he refused. Seeing that the officers on duty were taking no action, her relative eventually resorted to physical force in an attempt to protect her, she said.

Her relative has now been detained and sentenced to 15 days in jail for assaulting the man, she added.

“Then are we the ones who have committed a crime by trying to protect myself?” she asked again.

The woman also posed a series of questions to the public. She said the police officers on duty had not provided immediate assistance, leaving her no choice but to call a relative for protection. Was it wrong to take steps to ensure her own safety, she asked.

Her relative had stood up for her, she said, warning that a similar incident could happen to someone else in the future. Would people not seek to protect their own family members in such circumstances?

She said she had never expected to face harassment or humiliation after the incident. Why, then, had she been forced to go to the police station and court? Why had her relative been sentenced to 15 days in jail? Was protecting her his crime, she asked.

The woman said she had been told that the older man was suffering from a mental illness. But even if he had a mental health condition, she asked, did that give him the right to touch her inappropriately? Did that mean he was not responsible for his actions?

If the person accused of the offence had received a one-month jail sentence, she questioned, should the person who protested against the offence also be sentenced to 15 days in prison? Where, then, was her safety?

She said she was both the victim of the incident and someone who had subsequently faced harassment and humiliation. She questioned whether people could no longer protest against wrongdoing.

“Why should a woman have to face questions over her own dignity and safety?” she asked. “What have I done wrong? Is being born a woman itself a crime?”

She also questioned whether the person who commits an offence and the person who suffers it should be treated as equally guilty. What happened to her today, she said, could happen to other women in the future. Would people still blame those who stood up for them?

The woman said she had contacted the person who first posted the video on social media by phone and message, asking them to remove it for her safety. However, that person was unwilling to do so, she said.

She added that Dhanmondi police had arrived after the incident and arrested the older man. She had repeatedly told officers that she did not want to face further harassment, and they had assured her that she would be protected.

“Then why have I had to go through all this?” she asked.

The woman said she now felt as though she were the offender because her relative was being punished for trying to protect her. “Is this what justice under the law looks like?” she asked.

She said she had been enduring mental anguish since the incident and was appealing to the public for support. She did not want anyone to be punished for standing up for her, she said, and asked what she should do now and how she could protect her relative.

She also sought help for other people who might find themselves in similar circumstances.

item.title: Since when did disrespecting others become a source of income, asks Mehazabien
item.description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used to create objectionable images and videos by superimposing celebrities’ faces on other people’s content. These materials are then circulated on social media. Recently, several fake videos involving actresses Mehazabien Chowdhury and Pori Moni went viral, sparking widespread discussion and criticism. Mehazabien has now spoken out against the practice, asking, “ Since when did humiliating and disrespecting another person become a way to earn money?”

In a post on her Facebook page on Thursday morning, the actress expressed anger over the creation and circulation of fake content using AI. She questioned not only the conscience of those who create such material but also that of people who knowingly share it, helping it reach a wider audience.

On 13 October, objectionable videos featuring the names of Mehazabien and Pori Moni were circulated through the Instagram account of private television channel Maasranga Television. The channel later said its account had been hacked and that fake images and videos created through the misuse of AI technology had been posted. The organisation said it had recovered the account and removed the content.

Fact-checking organisation Rumor Scanner investigated the incident. In a report published on Wednesday, it said the videos in question were not real. They had been created by using face-swap technology to superimpose the two actresses’ faces onto other videos. Maasranga authorities also expressed regret over the incident and said they would take legal action.

Mehazabien shared her views on the issue on Thursday. At the beginning of her post, she wrote, “Creating false and fabricated content in someone’s name using AI and spreading it with the intention of humiliating them is not entertainment. It is a crime.”

However, her concern goes beyond the creation of fake content. She said when hundreds or thousands of people continue to share the same material, the issue goes beyond an individual’s wrongdoing and reflects a larger social problem. She also questioned the values of society in such circumstances.

The actress also rejected the common practice of urging people to consider how they would feel if the same thing happened to a family member. She wrote, “At this point, I don't even feel like repeating that old line that, ‘just imagine if this happened to your mother or sister’.”

Mehazabien then asked, “Why does someone have to be a member of our family for us to respect them as a human being?”

She also highlighted the competition for views, likes and shares on social media. According to her, the desire to remain trending or earn a few dollars by damaging someone else’s reputation is alarming. She acknowledged that content creation has become a source of livelihood for many people. However, she said the need to earn a living does not give anyone the right to humiliate another person.

Mehazabien said anyone could become a victim of such malicious content, noting that the issue is no longer limited to women or men. In the race for views and engagement, anyone can become involved in spreading harmful content, while anyone can also fall victim to it.

The actress said she was particularly concerned about people who do not create such content themselves but willingly spread it. Some share the material, others comment on it, while some help others access it. As a result, content created to humiliate one person reaches many more people.

Mehazabien has previously spoken out against the misuse of AI technology. Expressing concern over the circulation of manipulated images and videos of celebrities, she called for stricter laws, public awareness and accountability.

In Thursday’s post, however, the actress focused not only on the law but also on individuals’ personal responsibility. She said that misusing technology was wrong, and people also bore responsibility for helping spread that wrongdoing.

In the final line of her post, she directly addressed social media users, writing, “You may want to think about whether you want to become part of a criminal’s wrongdoing and reveal your own lack of conscience.”

item.title: Police disperse garment workers after nearly 4-hour road blockade in Uttara
item.description:
Police dispersed garment workers from the Azampur road in the capital’s Uttara area shortly before 11:45 am on Thursday, ending a blockade that had lasted nearly four hours.

The workers had occupied the road from 8:00 am, demanding payment of arrears, wage increases and other benefits, bringing traffic to a standstill on the Dhaka–Mymensingh highway and causing severe congestion.

Uttara West Police Station officer-in-charge Khalid Mansur confirmed the incident to Prothom Alo. He said traffic had come to a halt because the garment workers had occupied the road for an extended period.

As they refused to leave despite repeated requests, police dispersed them by chasing them away and firing sound grenades. Traffic resumed shortly before 11:45am, he added.

According to police and garment workers, employees from several factories began demonstrating on both sides of the highway near Azampur at around 8:30 am on Thursday, demanding payment of outstanding wages, higher pay and other benefits.

The workers had also staged protests on Tuesday and Wednesday over the same demands. Their demonstrations over three consecutive days severely disrupted traffic at key points along the Dhaka–Mymensingh highway.

With vehicles unable to move around Azampur and Rajlakkhi, severe congestion stretched from Uttara towards the airport road, causing considerable hardship for office-goers, commuters and pedestrians.

Worker Akhtar Hossain said the rising cost of essential goods had made it impossible to make ends meet on current wages. He said they had repeatedly appealed to the relevant authorities to settle their outstanding payments and address their demands, but received no resolution, leaving them with no choice but to take to the streets.

item.title: Writ seeks directives to protect cultural activities
item.description:
A writ petition has been filed seeking directives for preventive measures to protect lawful and peaceful cultural activities, including concerts, musical performances, folk music, Baul songs, theatrical productions, film screenings, traditional boat races and Pahela Baishakh (Bengali New Year) celebrations.

The petition also seeks directives to ensure preventive measures that protect artists, cultural workers, organisers and audiences from unlawful obstruction, intimidation, threats, violence, vandalism and coercion by unauthorised individuals or groups during such events.

Supreme Court lawyer Saddam Hossain (Abhi) filed the writ petition as the petitioner.

Confirming the filing on Wednesday, he told Prothom Alo, “The writ petition seeks directives for preventive measures to prevent obstruction to various cultural activities and events, including concerts, boat races, Pahela Baishakh celebrations and Baul music performances. It also seeks directives to ensure the protection and security of those involved in organising these events. The Supreme Court is currently in recess, and regular court proceedings will resume on 25 October. We will present the writ petition for a hearing before a regular bench.”

Earlier, on 9 September, lawyer Saddam Hossain sent a legal notice requesting the authorities to take necessary measures to protect lawful cultural events, including concerts, musical programmes, folk music performances, baul songs, theatre, film screenings, Pahela Baishakh celebrations and boat races, from threats and obstruction.

He sent the notice to three government secretaries and the Inspector General of Police.

The legal notice stated that incidents involving obstruction, objections and protests against cultural events, the suspension or cancellation of programmes on security grounds, and demands to stop traditional boat races had recently come to light in different parts of the country.

According to published reports, the authorities cancelled a concert in Kishoreganj in August 2026 following objections from a local group.

Around the same time, demands emerged to stop a traditional boat race on the Sunai River in Beanibazar, Sylhet. In Dhaka, a concert by singer Anupam Roy was cancelled at the last moment.

Lawyer Saddam Hossain said he filed the writ petition after receiving no response to the legal notice.

item.title: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Saudi Arabia has executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the Makkah region after a court convicted them of committing an “immoral act” inside a mosque, according to the country’s Ministry of Interior.
The ministry announced the executions on Wednesday, identifying the two as Nazerul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhtar, both Bangladeshi nationals, reports AJEL News.
According to the ministry’s statement, security authorities arrested the two following an investigation and referred their cases to a competent court.
The court found them guilty and sentenced them to death under discretionary punishment, citing the seriousness of the offence and the violation of the sanctity of the place and time.
The verdict was upheld by the relevant authorities, and a royal order was issued to carry out the sentences.
The executions took place in the Makkah region on Wednesday, the ministry said.

item.title: Uttara garment workers block Dhaka-Mymensingh highway for wage hike
item.description:
Several thousand garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway in the capital’s Uttara area on Thursday morning, demanding an increase in minimum wages, timely payment of wages and an end to arbitrary worker layoffs.
The blockade brought traffic on both sides of the highway to a complete standstill, triggering severe traffic congestion on the highway and surrounding roads and causing immense suffering to commuters, long-distance bus passengers and pedestrians.
Uttara West Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khalid said workers from various garment factories in Uttara began blocking the main road in Azampur area around 9:30am.
They later blocked the road near Rajlaxmi under Uttara West Police Station.
He estimated that 5,000 to 7,000 workers were occupying the roads, carrying sticks and other wooden objects.
Police have been deployed on both sides of the highway and are trying to persuade the workers to withdraw the blockade, the OC said.
He added that workers also blocked the road on Wednesday, but police later managed to clear it through persuasion.
Witnesses said workers from different garment factories have been staging demonstrations in various lanes of Uttara since Thursday morning before moving to the Azampur area and blocking the main road.
The blockade caused severe congestion on both sides of the Airport-Abdullahpur highway, leaving vehicles in long queues and disrupting movement across Uttara and adjacent areas.
Hundreds of passengers travelling on long-distance buses were stranded in traffic.
Unable to reach their destinations on time, many got off their buses and continued on foot, while commuters heading to work and people travelling for urgent purposes faced considerable hardship.

item.title: A major political test
item.description:
The standoff over the appointment of the vice-chancellor (VC) of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) has become more than an administrative dispute. It raises serious questions about the authority of university administrations, the dignity of academics, the limits of student protest, and the present government’s ability to implement its decisions.
If a VC is prevented from entering his workplace for weeks, and if reports that his electricity and water connections were cut are substantiated, the matter goes beyond ordinary campus dissent.
A university cannot function properly if administrative decisions are challenged through prolonged blockades rather than transparent institutional procedures.
The allegations deserve scrutiny, and the university community deserves a clear account of what has happened.
Dr Sheikh Shariful Islam was appointed VC by an order issued in the name of the president and went to CUET to assume his responsibilities. He is also a former student of the university. His appointment can be questioned, and students have every right to demand transparency.
However, if there are specific allegations against him, they should be made public and examined through appropriate procedures. Preventing an administrator from entering his workplace is not a substitute for evidence, due process, or accountability.
One of the most striking aspects of the controversy is that the previous VC, Dr Sayem, whose reinstatement is reportedly being demanded by protesters, was also appointed by the BNP government.
Why, then, is one appointment accepted while the other has triggered such prolonged resistance?
The difference may have an explanation, but it should be stated clearly and supported by evidence.
If the objection concerns administrative performance, protesters should identify the specific failures. If it concerns irregularities in the appointment process, evidence should be presented.
If the dispute is rooted in political affiliations or rival interests on campus, that too should be examined openly. Questions have been raised about the former VC’s political associations and alleged closeness to a particular political group.
Such claims should be investigated impartially, not treated as established facts. The same standards must apply to both the former and current administrations.
There is also a broader concern: Whether any political group is using the banner of ordinary students to advance its own interests.
That is a legitimate question in a politically-contested campus environment, but it cannot be answered by speculation or labels. Credible evidence is needed.
Student movements can be genuine expressions of grievance while also being vulnerable to political influence. Recognizing that possibility should lead to scrutiny, not assumptions about every participant.
The reported length of the standoff raises another difficult question. Why has a VC who reportedly served for only 56 days become the focus of such an intense confrontation?
What specific grievances have made a prolonged blockade necessary, and why have those grievances not been resolved through a transparent process?
The number of days served does not, by itself, prove that the protest is unjustified. It does, however, make a clear explanation of the dispute all the more important.
The government should not dismiss student concerns simply because an appointment was made under its authority. Nor should it allow pressure alone to determine whether an appointed official can perform his duties.
These principles are compatible: Investigate credible complaints, publish findings where appropriate, protect peaceful protest, and ensure that campus administration can function under established rules.
This is why CUET has become a political test for the government. If prolonged blockades are allowed to become an effective way of forcing administrative decisions, similar confrontations could emerge at other public universities.
The risk is not that every campus will repeat the same events, but that groups elsewhere may conclude that sustained pressure is more effective than formal complaints and institutional procedures.
The government’s responsibility is therefore twofold. It must provide students with a fair and credible channel to raise concerns, while also protecting the right of university officials to carry out their lawful responsibilities.
If the appointment process was flawed, the government should address that through the proper process. If allegations against the VC are not substantiated, it should explain why the appointment stands and take lawful steps to restore normal university operations. Neither force without scrutiny nor concession without evidence will resolve the underlying problem.
Universities should not be controlled by any political party, and no administration should be immune from criticism. But neither should a group be able to claim a veto over institutional decisions by keeping a campus in deadlock.
Academic freedom includes the freedom to question authority; it also depends on rules that protect students, teachers, and administrators from coercion.
The CUET controversy is about more than one appointment. It asks whether public universities in Bangladesh will be governed through evidence, institutional rules, and accountability, or whether administrative decisions will increasingly be shaped by blockades and organized pressure. The government’s response will help determine which precedent is set.
A credible investigation, transparent communication, and a lawful resolution are the way forward. The government must demonstrate that it can uphold institutional rules without suppressing legitimate dissent.
That is the real test. Not whether the government can win a confrontation, but whether it can ensure that universities remain places where disputes are resolved through evidence and due process rather than intimidation.
SK Arman Hossain is a policy analyst and a graduate student of public policy at the University of Erfurt, Germany. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Inside the collapse of education in the Rohingya camps
item.description:
Abdur Rashid keeps returning to the same subtraction.
He teaches at a learning centre inside Kutupalong Registered Camp , the settlement where he grew up after his family fled Myanmar, and the number he cannot make work is his own paycheck.
“I am not earning any fixed amount of salary from this community-led school. My earnings depend on the payment possible to gather from different families in this camp,” Rashid says.
“If I could teach at any learning centres under a donor-funded learning program, I might earn a stipend of around Tk 13,000 for teaching as a volunteer,” he said, describing the opportunity he lost.
Many Rohingya teachers like him have had to face this reality in Cox’s Bazar since 2025.
Rashid finished his primary schooling in camp, then pushed through years of paperwork and travel restrictions to earn a bachelor’s degree from local colleges in Cox’s Bazar.
Now, he is managing a community-led school that Rohingya families increasingly treat as their only dependable option.
He is careful not to call this progress.
“When formal donor funding began to falter, educated community members stepped forward to keep our children learning,” he says.
“That stepping-in comes at a cost that families absorb directly, rather than through an aid budget.”
Families in his network pay roughly $0.50 to $6.50 a month to keep whiteboards, markers, and modest teacher stipends flowing.
It is a system built out of necessity rather than design, and Rashid is one of thousands of Rohingya educators now holding it together by hand.
A system built for emergency, not permanence
When more than 730,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State in 2017, aid agencies opened temporary learning centres within months, teaching basic literacy in Burmese, English, and math.
Initially, children were taught using an informal curriculum called the Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA).
This curriculum attempted to include Burmese, English, and Mathematics; many teachers recruited from the host community were entirely unequipped to teach in Burmese.
The curriculum failed to reconcile the spoken Rohingya dialect with Burmese written script, creating severe comprehension barriers for children.
Later on, the Bangladesh government and Unicef launched a Myanmar Curriculum by late 2021, expanding coverage toward all 410,000 school-age children in the camps through 3,200 learning centres.
A record 300,000 children enrolled in school in 2023-24, the first time Rohingya children of all ages were studied under one standardized curriculum. A dedicated campaign pulled 13,000 out-of-school children into classrooms.
However, this learning framework, temporary by design, was meant not to function as a real school network.
Host-community and Rohingya teachers taught children only five subjects through instruction in Burmese and English.
They progressed automatically through grades without formal examinations.
When the money stopped
The arithmetic Rashid does every month became the arithmetic of the entire humanitarian sector in June 2025.
The $300 million USAid fund in 2024 had fallen to $12m in June 2025.
By April, the humanitarian education sector had secured only $22m of its required $72m.
The cutbacks affected more than 6,400 learning centres across 33 camps, home to over 1.2 million people, pushing roughly 300,000 of the camps’ 437,000 school-age children out of classrooms.
Around 1,250 teachers lost their jobs overnight when Unicef and Save the Children suspended all donor-funded learning programs.
“When funds from major bilateral donors are reduced overnight, agencies face excruciating trade-offs. You cannot strip a family of their minimum 1,900-calorie daily food ration or shut down cholera treatment facilities.”
A knowledge management officer with Unicef Bangladesh in Cox’s Bazar, speaking confidentially, explained the rationale plainly.
“Education, while vital for long-term human development, is treated as a secondary priority during acute budget shortfalls.”
The community steps in
What replaced the closed centres was not a plan. It was families like the ones Rashid works with. They quietly rebuilt a parallel system out of tuition fees and volunteer labour.
These community-run schools now operate on something close to a private micro-school model, staffed by educators who completed their own upper-secondary schooling and teach one subject at a time.
The clearest sign that this parallel system now sees itself as permanent came in March 2026, when the newly formed Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees held its first matriculation exams, with question papers handed to Bangladesh’s Armed Police Battalion for secure delivery across camp exam centres.
Fifty three community-run schools joined the board at its founding, and the network now covers kindergarten through grade twelve with free enrolment.
It offers something the old learning centres never could: A certificate a student can actually hold onto.
A script they were never taught
Rohingya children in Myanmar were denied both Burmese literacy and any formal way to write their own language for decades.
Even a decade ago, aid workers were warning that most children were adopting Bengali instead , simply because it was more useful day-to-day than their mother tongue.
That changed in 2024, when Children on the Edge, a child rights organization, piloted mother-tongue lessons in Hanifi script across its Kutupalong and Bhasan Char classrooms, training more than 70 teachers for a program that now reaches over 6,300 children .
The Hanifi Rohingya script, developed in the 1980s and added to the Unicode standard in 2018, gave the language a modern, typeable form for the first time; it took years before any classroom actually taught it.
Even so, the shift remains marginal in light of the crisis; nearly 50 community schools teach the script at all, and most learning centres and madrasas still default to Burmese or Bengali, the languages of the systems around them rather than the language of the children inside them.
Where the mosque becomes the classroom
Many parents have expressed frustration with donor-funded learning centres, as they focus heavily on play-based learning and basic alphabet skills without offering a clear path to high school.
Parents in refugee camps prefer madrasas over donor-funded learning centres due to deep-seated cultural, structural, and operational differences. They worry that temporary frameworks will dilute traditional community values.
Religious learning in madrasas has deep roots in Rohingya communities that predate the 2017 exodus, and the camps’ network, running through neighbourhood maktabs and a formal examining body called Wifaq al-Madaris al-Arabia al-Rohingiya , has expanded quietly through years when donor-funded classrooms were closing.
Unlike the learning centres, madrasas generally do not require birth registration or other legal documentation many refugee families lack, and they are funded privately, often by donors in Saudi Arabia and Turkey rather than through the camps’ formal humanitarian architecture.
An education sector specialist who is sceptical of madrasas as a systemic fix concedes the pull is genuine.
“Madrasas are deeply embedded in the cultural landscape, but they cannot serve as a structural replacement for formal education,” the specialist said.
“They lack a standardized curriculum, formal learning outcome assessments, and recognized pathways toward higher education.”
As Cox’s Bazar nears a decade of hosting the mass influx of Rohingya refugees, the prolonged decay of primary education threatens not only the immediate welfare of children but the future stability of the entire region.
The existing learning framework currently provided to Rohingya children offers no viable long-term future.
Without funding commitment, the half-built futures of Rohingya children will remain permanently stalled in the muddy hills of Cox’s Bazar, leaving an entire generation stranded between a homeland they cannot return to and a world that has turned its back on their education.
Rashid does not need that document to know what adjustment and funding shifts look like from inside a classroom.
What thousands of teachers like him have built is not a fix for what donors walked away from. It is the measure of what remains in their hands.
Zulker Naeen is a Research Coordinator, Centre for Critical and Qualitative Studies (CQS) and Adjunct Faculty, Department of Media Studies and Journalism (MSJ), University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). This report features interviews and infographics by Md. Mahfuzar Rahman, Shahriar Sarker, Shihab Shahriar, Sumaya Parvez, and Quazi Moyeen Ahmed for the Data Journalism Course at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Is AI the ultimate solution?
item.description:
In today’s world of the internet, social media, and various streaming platforms, our daily lives have fully submitted to technology. It’s not been too long ago that we were introduced to the internet, and today, most if not all of us are using it every day.
Recently, there have been a lot of AI trends and challenges going viral, where the user needs to upload a photo on ChatGPT to get a modified and edited photo. They share these photos on social media for the sole purpose of “fun.” However, the aftermath of that one picture is more than one can imagine.
To talk about the effects of using AI will be a long conversation with plenty of controversial and political agendas. With increased use of AI, we, as its users, are only providing more data to the big tech companies like Google and Meta who benefit with every click, every upload, and every engagement by collecting our personal information.
The individuals in authority of these personal data ultimately are invading people’s privacy and dehumanizing them by abusing their power. The collected data could be nothing but just the age of the user or their gender, but there are multiple ways this information is misused.
We know that there are various facial recognition machines being used for every sector. The data collected through these machines are processed to develop generati ve AI along with making weapons.
Another thing that helps AI and its function is algorithms. We know the word algorithm as something that helps curate our social media pages. Every ‘like’, ‘share’, or any engagement done on social media helps create data which the algorithm picks up as the user's information.
Each unique page is the result of an algorithm after understanding the user's interests through collected data. But algorithms do not only work on social media but rather, work beyond just our social media explore pages.
Every piece of information forms a code that AI tools read and gather in their system. The use of AI or any other technology is not as simple as we think.
Advanced technologies were invented with the purpose of making everyone’s daily work a bit easier. But it is important that as users, we educate ourselves with its uses, functions, and effects.
When these technologies are marketed, they are presented as tools to make our lives easier. Yet, we are never given a manual on how to use it. Furthermore, we are unaware of what they are doing after collecting our personal information.
Many use generative AI for help when they are stuck with work. Students, corporate workers, even people working in creative sectors use generative AI for their daily tasks.
But running to ChatGPT for every single task is not only dangerous, it is also damaging our ability to think creatively.
Looking back at the history of ChatGPT trends, the first one that became viral and concerning was transforming personal photos into “Ghibli style” images. People were paying for ChatGPT subscriptions only to edit their picture to look like a scene from a Ghibli movie.
This was very disappointing for the artists, animators, illustrators, and every other individual who sometimes worked for months just to draw a frame of these movies.
The Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki expressed his disappointment, talking about how this is disrespectful to everyone working in the animation industry.
Looking at the situation now, it seems like we as a society are not educated enough to understand how much our actions are damaging our future with our AI usage.
We need to comprehend that the use of generative AI, which people use only for “fun,” has negative effects beyond what we often imagine. It is simultaneously damaging the ecological balance of the climate and harming every living being on this planet.
People should be more conscious and aware of every action, and ask questions about whether we are harming anyone or not. With our daily lives being so dependent on online platforms and services, we should not be jumping into participating in any viral trend.
It is unavoidable to use advanced technologies. However, it should not come at the expense of our ability to imagine and create.
We should always remember that AI or any technological tools are made by humans. It is us humans who program them for our use. We should not let technology take over our lives.
Let us all as a society become more aware of the functions and effects of AI, or any advanced technologies before blindly using them. The increased use of advanced technologies is not the solution to all our problems. Rather, it could be inviting the end of everything sooner than we can imagine.
Nushin Tarannum Lamia is a graduate student of Communication Culture and Media at Drexel University, Philadelphia, USA.

item.title: Addressing our plastic crisis
item.description:
Bangladesh’s decision to launch a national platform to tackle plastic pollution is a welcome step towards addressing one of the country’s most persistent environmental challenges.
However, its success will depend on whether we see real commitment to concrete action rather than it becoming another initiative that produces discussions without meaningful results.
Plastic pollution has become an increasingly visible threat across Bangladesh, with plastic waste continuing to damage ecosystems and threaten public health. Excessive reliance on single-use plastics, poor waste management, and inadequate recycling facilities have allowed the problem to grow.
The consequences affect everyone -- particularly communities whose livelihoods depend on healthy waterways and a clean environment.
Bringing together government agencies, businesses, development partners, and civil society can therefore help improve coordination and promote a circular economy.
However, consumers cannot be expected to shoulder the responsibility alone. Manufacturers, importers, and brand owners must also be held accountable for the waste generated by their products.
The government must establish clear targets for reducing plastic use, expanding recycling, and improving waste collection. Existing regulations must be enforced consistently, with meaningful penalties for non-compliance. Businesses should be encouraged to reduce unnecessary packaging and invest in reusable alternatives.
Without effective monitoring, even well-intentioned policies will struggle to deliver lasting change.
Waste collectors, sorters and recyclers also have a role to play. Many work in unsafe conditions without adequate protection or recognition, and improving their working conditions and integrating them into formal waste management systems would strengthen the country’s recycling capacity.
Public awareness must be prioritized, along with adequate collection facilities and stronger enforcement. Local authorities need sufficient resources to manage waste effectively, while households and businesses must have accessible disposal options.
This platform presents an opportunity to coordinate efforts and establish accountability across sectors. Its success must include reduced plastic waste, higher recycling rates, and cleaner rivers and neighbourhoods.
Bangladesh cannot afford another initiative that exists only on paper.

item.title: Rural women have shaped our country
item.description:
The International Day of Rural Women, observed today, is an opportunity to recognize the contributions of women to rural communities -- especially in Bangladesh, where recognition remains far removed from their lived reality.
Despite their contributions to agriculture, household economies, and community life, rural women continue to be marginalized, with limited access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making.
Women play a significant role in Bangladesh’s agricultural sector -- yet female farmers often remain invisible in a system that frequently acknowledges men as the primary agricultural workers. Their labour is undervalued, and many lack ownership of the land they cultivate.
Without land titles, access to institutional credit, quality seeds, modern equipment, and agricultural training, they are left at a disadvantage despite their essential contributions to food security.
This inequality extends beyond farming: Rural women often face barriers to education, healthcare, formal employment, and financial services.
For women in climate-vulnerable areas, floods, cyclones, and river erosion add another layer of insecurity, threatening livelihoods and increasing the burden of keeping families afloat.
Addressing these challenges requires more than celebrating women once a year. Female farmers must be formally recognized in agricultural policies and included in training programs, subsidies, and credit schemes.
Ensuring women's access to land ownership and inheritance rights is equally important. Local government institutions must also create opportunities for rural women to participate meaningfully in decisions that affect their lives.
Furthermore, investments in rural education, healthcare, childcare, and safe employment can help women move beyond economic dependence. Support for women-led cooperatives and small businesses would also help create sustainable livelihoods.
Bangladesh cannot achieve inclusive development while a substantial part of its rural workforce remains overlooked. Rural women are active contributors to our economic development, and their labour must be valued, their rights protected, and their voices heard.
The true measure of this day will be whether recognition translates into lasting changes in their everyday lives.

item.title: Indian national arrested at Dhaka airport with 4.28kg of kush
item.description:
The Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) has arrested an Indian national at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka with 4.28kg of kush allegedly concealed beneath Indian saris in his trolley bag.
The man was detained on Wednesday afternoon at the airport’s green channel in the arrival hall. A subsequent search of his trolley led to the recovery of the drugs.
The arrestee, Abhijit Das, 40, is a resident of North 24 Parganas district in West Bengal, India.
Authorities also seized an Indian passport, 2,160 Indian rupees, 70 Thai baht, a smartphone, a boarding pass and three Indian saris from him.
Deputy Director Md Rajiur Rahman of the DNC’s Dhaka Metro (North) office said a special team led by Dr Md Abu Saeed Mia, assistant director of the DNC’s airport office, took position at the green channel around 1pm following intelligence inputs.
Das, who arrived from Bangkok on Thai Airways flight TG 321, was detained on suspicion, he said.
Witnesses and representatives of various agencies at the airport searched the trolley, leading to the recovery of 4kg 280g of kush concealed beneath the clothes.
During preliminary interrogation, Das identified himself as a porter at Bongaon railway station in India, Rajiur Rahman said.
According to the DNC official, Das claimed that an international drug trafficking network operating across three countries recruits low-income people in India to transport drugs from Kolkata to Bangkok. The drugs are then allegedly smuggled into Bangladesh concealed among goods, including Indian saris.
Rajiur Rahman said preliminary questioning suggested the network was attempting to establish a market for kush in Bangladesh.
A case has been filed against Das at the airport police station under the relevant provisions of the Narcotics Control Act, 2018, as amended in 2026, he added.

item.title: CNG driver injured in cocktail blast outside July Memorial Museum
item.description:
A CNG-run auto-rickshaw driver was injured in a cocktail explosion outside Gate 1 of the July Memorial Museum in Dhaka’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area on Wednesday night.
The injured man, Md Shahin, also known as Arif Molla, 45, was taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital before being transferred to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital for further treatment.
The incident occurred around 11pm on Wednesday.
Sub-Inspector Md Mahbub Alam of Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station said unidentified assailants hurled two cocktails outside the museum’s Gate 1, one of which exploded. Shahin, who was standing nearby, was injured by splinters.
“After receiving the news, we rushed him to safety and first took him to Shaheed Suhrawardy Hospital. From there, he was brought to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for better treatment the same night, and he is now under treatment,” he said.
The motive behind the attack and the identities of those involved remain unknown, the police officer said. Police are reviewing CCTV footage from the surrounding area to identify the attackers.
Shahin is the son of the late Bhola Sheikh and hails from Salimabad village in Nagarpur upazila of Tangail. He was staying at a CNG garage in Jatrabari.

item.title: Vinicius banned for four games after hair-pulling red card
item.description:
Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior will miss the upcoming Clasico in La Liga against Barcelona after being issued a four-match suspension on Wednesday following his red card for hair-pulling against Villarreal last week.
The Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee confirmed the Brazilian will be banned for several matches including the visit to face league leaders Barca on October 25 for both the red card and his subsequent protests.
The committee said Vinicius had been suspended for two games for "behaving violently... (while) not being in a position to challenge for the ball" and a further two matches for "protests" to the officials.
As well as the Clasico, Vinicius will be unavailable to face Sevilla (October 18), Racing Santander (November 1) and Valencia (November 7) in La Liga.
Despite Vinicius's red card against Villarreal, Jose Mourinho's fourth-place Madrid earned a 1-0 win to stay six points behind Barcelona.
The 26-year-old winger reacted angrily to the decision, made after a VAR review, which also chalked off a goal he had scored in the aftermath of his pull on Nathan Saliba's hair.
Vinicius had to be held back by his team-mates as he remonstrated with referee Isidro Diaz de Mera.
Mourinho, also upset by the officiating, refused to participate in his post-match press conference.
Vinicius apologised to his teammates and Madrid supporters after the match. "I am sorry to the team and the fans," he wrote on social media.
The attacker has endured a difficult start to the campaign, scoring just once in nine appearances, and was dropped to the bench against Villarreal, with his red card occurring around 20 minutes after he was introduced as a substitute.
Madrid's visit to Camp Nou will be Mourinho's first Clasico since returning as coach of Los Blancos this summer.
Thus far Hansi Flick's Barcelona, back-to-back Spanish champions, boast a perfect record of 10 wins from 10 matches this season across all competitions.

item.title: Six-star Villa make history with stunning Fenerbahce rout
item.description:
Aston Villa recorded their biggest ever European victory as Nicolas Jackson inspired a 6-0 rout of Fenerbahce in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Unai Emery's side won at Villa Park for the first time this season to maintain their 100 percent start in Europe's elite club competition.
Swiss forward Johan Manzambi put Villa in front and Jackson was on target twice before the interval.
Ross Barkley's second-half double and Tammy Abraham's late strike put the seal on a welcome success on home turf for Villa.
Villa Park's North Stand is currently closed for building work as the club increases the stadium's capacity to over 50,000.
Amid suggestions that the reduced crowd and lack of noise was affecting Villa's players, Emery had said there were "no excuses" for failing to win any of their previous three home games.
Languishing in 16th place in the Premier League, Villa responded to Emery's demand for a more intense performance as they extended their unbeaten run to four games in all competitions.
"Overall it was a very good match. There are still things to improve. It was a strong result for us," Emery said.
"Keep going forward. It helps confidence for us. We did some changes to get other players confidence and minutes. What we did today was fantastic. The Champions League is very difficult."
Following a summer of upheaval featuring the sales of star players including Ollie Watkins and Ezri Konsa, the Europa League holders are finally emerging from a turbulent period.
Saluting Jackson's contribution, Emery added: "He has power to get in behind. He can drop and help as well.
"We need him always to be in the box when we're attacking. Jackson is our striker."
- Unstoppable Jackson -
Villa captain John McGinn fired narrowly wide and Ibrahim Mbaye tested Ederson with a long-range blast in a frenetic opening.
Villa were rewarded for their early barrage in the 12th minute.
Matteo Guendouzi's wayward header fell to Manzambi, who took a touch before unloading a powerful shot that took a deflection off Milan Skriniar as it whistled past the wrong-footed Ederson.
Manzambi, 21, is the second player to score on his Champions League debut on his birthday.
Jackson's low strike was pushed away by Ederson, but the Senegal striker wasn't to be denied.
After Fenerbahce surrendered possession carelessly in the 31st minute, Boubacar Kamara's pass found Jackson on the edge of the area and he guided a fine finish past Ederson.
Jackson was proving unstoppable and the 25-year-old made it three after 39 minutes.
Taking aim from 18 yards, Jackson's low drive carried too much power for Ederson, who could only parry it into the net.
It was Jackson's fifth goal in eight games since arriving from Chelsea in August.
Villa also scored three times in the first half when they won at Club Brugge in their opening game of the Champions League group phase.
Playing his first match in England for four years following his troubled spell at Manchester United, Fenerbahce forward Mason Greenwood was booed mercilessly by Villa fans.
In between the taunts, they were able to celebrate two more goals in the second half.
Barkley slotted home from the penalty spot after Ismail Yuksek fouled Manzambi.
And Barkley struck again four minutes later, meeting Mbaye's cross with a shot that deflected in off Bartug Elmaz.
Abraham came off the bench to wrap up Villa's record win as he tapped in Alysson's cross in stoppage time.

item.title: Messi inspires Miami to playoff-clinching victory
item.description:
Lionel Messi set up a Rodrigo De Paul goal and German Berterame snapped his scoring drought as Inter Miami booked their place in the MLS playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday.
Victory gave Cristian 'Kily' Gonzalez his first back-to-back wins since taking over as head coach last month, guaranteeing second-placed Miami at least a place in the wild card round, with five games left to play.
"I'm leaving happy. Obviously, there's a lot to improve, but we're making progress little by little," Gonzalez said.
Messi -- who had scored twice on Saturday after returning to his club side from last week's emotional Argentina send-off -- was again a dangerous presence, playing a hand in both first-half goals.
In the 20th minute Messi trapped the ball just outside the penalty area and passed it to De Paul, who found Suarez on the byline with a diagonal looping ball.
Suarez rolled it flat across the face of the goal, giving Berterame a simple finish for his first goal since May.
De Paul grabbed Miami's second on a quick counter with the final kick of the first half. Berterame brought the ball across the halfway line and was slightly fortunate to find Messi to his right with a mishit pass.
Messi drew in three defenders then laid it off with the outside of his left foot to De Paul, who slammed it high to the keeper's right.
In a goalless second half, Messi sent a curling effort from just outside the box over the bar.
As the game clock hit 90, Messi played a short corner to De Paul, who unleashed a shot from outside the box toward the far top corner. United States national team goalkeeper Matt Freese made a superb diving save, tipping the ball onto the post.
New York City, on a dire streak of just one win in their last 11 MLS games, at least had a chance for a consolation deep in stoppage time with a penalty.
Ian Fray brought down fellow substitute Talles Magno, who turned sharply away from goal and ran into the defender's trailing leg.
But Dayne St. Clair made a brilliant save, flinging himself low and right to palm the ball around the bar.
It was Inter Miami's second straight clean sheet, after none in their previous 10.
"I really liked how we handled dropping back into defensive shape. We didn't get caught out on the counter and were very aggressive, breaking up plays whenever a sudden transition from them looked likely," said Gonzalez.
"Perhaps our ball circulation was a bit too slow at times, but that's just how the game played out."
Even with first-place Nashville out of sight this year in the Eastern Conference, the win consolidated Miami's grip on second, and home-field advantage into the playoffs.

item.title: PSG 'got lucky' to win City thriller, says Luis Enrique
item.description:
Paris Saint-Germain boss Luis Enrique said the European champions rode their luck to beat Manchester City 4-2 and maintain a perfect start to their defence of the Champions League.
The visitors ran riot in the first half of City's first home game since being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules as they raced into a 3-0 lead.
Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha were on target in a near flawless first 45 minutes by the French champions.
But City roared back after the break as Erling Haaland struck twice, while they also hit the woodwork twice and were denied by a brilliant goalline clearance by Nuno Mendes.
"We could have lost this match if they scored the chances that they created," said Luis Enrique.
"I think it was a very nice match, but the way they play, it's amazing. We like to play these kind of matches."
Maghnes Akliouche briefly restored PSG's three-goal lead in the second half, while Ferran Torres also missed a late penalty for the visitors.
"We try to win every single match. We try to score. We don't stop if we score one or two goals," added Luis Enrique.
"It's very nice to feel that but I have to repeat, today we were lucky because in the second half we could have conceded more goals."
Enzo Maresca had made a perfect start to the daunting challenge of replacing Pep Guardiola as City manager by winning his first eight games in all competitions.
Guardiola, who won 20 trophies in a 10-year spell at City, made his return to the Etihad Stadium in a show of support after City were found guilty on more than 100 charges of financial impropriety between 2009 and 2018.
But he saw his former players fall to their first defeat of the season despite a spirited fightback after being thoroughly outplayed in the first half.
"From tonight we can learn many things," said Maresca. "Even if we concede two goals (in two minutes) against the best team in Europe, we need to continue.
"I try to continue to learn from the players because I just arrived three months ago, but the feeling at the moment is very good."
Victory took PSG top of the Champions League table after two games, while City drop to 17th.

item.title: PSG beat City in Champions League thriller, Barcola hits Liverpool hat-trick
item.description:
Reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory away to embattled Manchester City in the UEFA Champions League on Wednesday, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over LASK in Austria.
Elsewhere on a prolific night of European action, Real Madrid came from 3-1 down to beat Roma 4-3 and Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park.
City were playing at home at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since being found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over almost a decade that have left them facing the prospect of severe sanctions.
That verdict appeared to be hanging over the City team as PSG raced into a three-goal lead just past the half-hour mark, with Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha all netting for the French side.
With former boss Pep Guardiola watching on, City produced a second-half fightback as Erling Haaland scored twice to take him to four Champions League goals already this season.
However, PSG got a fourth in between the Norwegian's strikes, with City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma unable to keep out a Maghnes Akliouche shot.
Donnarumma later made some amends by saving a Ferran Torres penalty, but City succumbed by the same margin as in their last Champions League meeting with PSG in January 2025.
"In the first half we were far superior to a great City side," Paris coach Luis Enrique told broadcaster Canal Plus. "You can think these games are over but it is never the case at this level, and we could have ended up losing."
Back-to-back title-holders PSG have won both Champions League games this season, scoring 10 goals in the process. They face Barcelona next week.
"Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more," City coach Enzo Maresca told TNT Sports.
Barcola, a big-money summer signing from PSG, had not found the net for Liverpool before scoring three times at the Raiffeisen Arena after Ronald Araujo had broken the deadlock against the Austrian champions.
Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas also netted for Andoni Iraola's side, who were 4-0 ahead at one point before LASK scored three times in the space of 15 second-half minutes through Robert Ljubicic and Florian Flecker's brace.
"Obviously I think he has to enjoy this because to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult," said Iraola of France forward Barcola.
- Real late show, Villa hit six -
There was a dramatic denouement in Italy, where a Marten de Roon goal and a Donyell Malen brace had Roma 3-1 up against Real Madrid inside the final 10 minutes.
However the visitors, who had earlier seen Kylian Mbappe score on his 100th Champions League appearance, produced an incredible late fightback.
Carlos Espi pulled one back in the 82nd minute and Brazil forward Endrick equalised before Antonio Rudiger grabbed a last-minute winner for Jose Mourinho's men.
Swiss international Johan Manzambi opened the scoring for Villa against Fenerbahce on his 21st birthday, setting his club up for their biggest ever European victory.
Nicolas Jackson scored twice before half-time, and Ross Barkley bagged a second-half brace including a penalty. Tammy Abraham completed the scoring, leaving the Turkish side stunned.
Fredrik Sjovold got the only goal of the game as Norway's Bodo/Glimt beat former European champions Borussia Dortmund 1-0, while Real Betis beat Porto 3-2 in Spain.
Abde Ezzalzouli put Betis ahead just after half-time, only for Gabri Veiga and Samuel Aghehowa to hit back for the Portuguese champions. However, Juan Hernandez levelled again and veteran Isco got a late winner.
In Rotterdam, Feyenoord beat Como 3-2 as the Dutch side's coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst got the better of Cesc Fabregas.
Assane Diao gave the Italians the lead but Gjivai Zechiel and Anis Hadj Moussa struck for Feyenoord before an own goal by goalkeeper Robert Sanchez made it 3-1. Anastasios Douvikas then pulled one back.
Ukraine's Shakhtar Donetsk were playing at home for the first time at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge stadium, and they marked the occasion with a 3-1 win over AEK Athens.
Lovro Majer gave AEK the lead, but a Pedrinho penalty levelled matters before Vinicius Tobias and Gleiker Mendoza sealed the win to leave Shakhtar on four points from two outings.
Stuttgart won 3-0 away to Slovan Bratislava in the night's other game.
